main_point: A class action lawsuit led by the estate of jazz musician Chet Baker and collective societies alleges that major Canadian record labels have failed to pay royalties for hundreds of thousands of works, potentially resulting in billions in penalties, while the industry defends its practices by citing a 'pending list' of unlicensed works and dismissing the lawsuit as exaggerated.

statements.text: Under the Class Proceedings Act of 1992, a copyright lawsuit involving Canada's largest music industry players could result in penalties exceeding one billion dollars if the legal team's claims regarding unpaid royalties for hundreds of thousands of works are substantiated.
statements.text_short: A copyright lawsuit under Canada's Class Proceedings Act could impose over a billion dollars in penalties on major music labels.

statements.text: On October 6, the estate of the late jazz artist Chet Baker updated and refiled a class action suit. This legal action targets four large Canadian record labels and their parent firms. The lawsuit claims these companies did not pay royalties for hundreds of thousands of musical works.
statements.text_short: Chet Baker's estate filed an amended class action lawsuit against major Canadian record labels for unpaid royalties on hundreds of thousands of works.

statements.actor: Society for Reproduction Rights of Authors (SODRAC)
actor_aliases: Society for Reproduction Rights of Authors (SODRAC)
statements.text: The Society for Reproduction Rights of Authors (SODRAC), which was initially named as a defendant in the copyright lawsuit, switched sides in January to join the plaintiffs alongside the estate of Chet Baker and other rightsholders in suing the major record labels.
statements.text_short: SODRAC switched from being a defendant to joining the plaintiffs in the copyright lawsuit against major record labels.

actor_aliases: the late jazz musician Chet Baker
statements.text: The estate of Chet Baker views the 'pending list'—a record of works not correctly licensed for reproduction maintained by the Canadian Musical Reproduction Rights Agency—as clear evidence of copyright infringement by the major record labels.
statements.text_short: Chet Baker's estate views the 'pending list' of unlicensed works as evidence of copyright infringement by major record labels.

statements.text: The four major Canadian record labels assert that developing internal systems to resolve the backlog of unlicensed works is economically unfeasible, a stance that the lawsuit's author argues contradicts the plaintiffs' evidence of the labels' refusal to cooperate in fixing the problem.
statements.text_short: Major Canadian record labels claim internal fixes for unlicensed works are too costly, contradicting the lawsuit's evidence of their refusal to cooperate.

statements.text: The class action lawsuit against major Canadian record labels relies on statutory damages of CA$500 to $20,000 per unlicensed work, while the industry defends its position by citing a history of a flawed compulsory license scheme that was later replaced by the current mechanical license system.
statements.text_short: The lawsuit seeks massive statutory damages for unlicensed works, while the industry defends its practices by citing a history of a flawed licensing system.

statements.text: The current Mechanical Licensing Agreement between the Canadian Musical Reproduction Rights Agency and the Canadian Recording Industry Association expired on December 31, 2012, following a series of earlier terms set in 1990, 1998, 2004, 2006, and 2008.
statements.text_short: The current licensing agreement between the Canadian collective society and major record labels expired in December 2012 after several previous iterations.

statements.text: Under the current licensing framework, the Canadian Musical Reproduction Rights Agency and the Society for Reproduction Rights of Authors are contractually required to provide lists of all collections they represent to record labels, while the labels must supply copies of released material to permit content assessment.
statements.text_short: The licensing framework requires Canadian collective societies to provide collection lists to labels, while labels must supply copies of released material for assessment.

statements.text: The current Mechanical Licensing Agreement between the Canadian Recording Industry Association and the collective societies is structured so broadly that it legally prevents any party from refusing to grant a license, while simultaneously requiring record labels to submit quarterly lists of unlicensed works to facilitate royalty collection by the societies.
statements.text_short: The current licensing agreement prevents labels from refusing licenses and mandates quarterly pending list submissions for royalty collection.

statements.text: In January 2009, Alain Lauzon, who serves as the General Manager of the Society for Reproduction Rights of Authors, Composers and Publishers, officially filed a supplementary affidavit. This document was intended to add his organization as a plaintiff in the class action lawsuit targeting major Canadian record labels over the issue of unpaid royalties.
statements.text_short: SODRAC's General Manager formally joined the lawsuit against major record labels as a plaintiff in January 2009.

statements.text: Drawing on his expertise as a qualified Chartered Accountant with over two decades of experience managing industry-wide music licensing, Alain Lauzon asserts that his organization represents a significant portion of Canadian musical works and confirms that major record labels bear the legal and customary responsibility for obtaining mechanical licenses.
statements.text_short: An expert in music licensing confirms that major labels are legally responsible for obtaining mechanical licenses for Canadian works.

statements.text: Reinforcing the legal and customary obligation of record labels to secure mechanical licenses, Alain Lauzon, representing the collective society, states with professional confidence that the industry has generally failed to take necessary steps to resolve the persistent problem of unlicensed works.
statements.text_short: A specialist in the field states that music companies have mostly been unable to fix the issue of unauthorized recordings.

statements.text: The Canadian Recording Industry Association (CRIA) representative, Don Hogarth, directed a response to a blog post by the CRIA's own lobbyist, Barry Sookman, instead of answering the specific questions posed by the media. This decision to rely on a blog entry written by an industry insider, rather than providing direct answers, suggests an attempt to deflect scrutiny from the lawsuit's allegations of unpaid royalties. Given that the blog post contains numerous factual inaccuracies and misdirecting statements, this approach risks further misleading the public and undermining the credibility of the industry's defense against the claims of unpaid mechanical royalties.
statements.text_short: The CRIA representative deflected media scrutiny by directing responses to an industry lobbyist's inaccurate blog post instead of answering specific questions.

statements.text: David A. Basskin, a lawyer and industry insider representing the Canadian Mechanical Reproduction Rights Agency (CMRRA), argues that the four major record labels in Canada have actively resisted and failed to negotiate a licensing system for twenty years. This resistance has prevented the collective societies from securing adequate measures to mechanically license musical works and collect the fees and royalties owed to rights holders. The statement frames the industry's refusal to adapt to the growing use of digital services as the primary cause of the ongoing financial dispute and unpaid debts.
statements.text_short: The CMRRA representative argues that major record labels have resisted and failed to negotiate a fair licensing system for twenty years, causing unpaid royalties.

statements.text: The value of the list of unlicensed musical works is increasing by over C$1.1 million every quarter, a trend that indicates the four major record labels will owe at least C$73 million in outstanding debt by the end of 2012. This rapid growth in the pending list demonstrates that the industry's failure to mechanically license works and pay due fees is accelerating the financial liability, contradicting claims that the situation is stable or manageable. The data suggests that without immediate and comprehensive action to resolve the licensing backlog, the penalties for the class action lawsuit will reach billions of dollars.
statements.text_short: The rising value of the unlicensed works list indicates that major record labels face massive future debt, contradicting claims that the licensing backlog is manageable.
